title: Ship 42: in orbit after Flight 15, catch still ahead
seoTitle: Ship 42 Flight 15: in orbit, booster diverted, Saturday catch
description: Ship 42 launched on Starship Flight 15 at about 4:47 p.m. CT on 13 Nov 2026. Super Heavy diverted to the Gulf. The Ship is in orbit with 26 Starlink V3s deployed, and a tower catch is still planned Saturday if systems stay healthy.
ogImageAlt: Ship 42 launch title card on a dark background with the Supercharged Daily bolt
afterSub: Booster diverted. Ship 42 is coasting toward a Saturday catch if systems stay healthy. See the updates log.
featureGo: In orbit: the flight so far and Saturday's Ship catch →
summary: Ship 42 launched on Starship Flight 15 from Pad 2 at Starbase on Friday 13 November 2026, at about 4:47 p.m. CT (22:47 UTC), according to Space.com's live coverage of SpaceX's webcast. Super Heavy Booster 22 diverted to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf. SpaceX later said the booster automatically aborted the Pad 2 catch because of a guidance, navigation and control issue, as relayed by NASASpaceflight quoting Dan Huot.

Ship 42 reached orbit — only the second Starship to do so — and deployed all 26 Starlink V3 satellites. SpaceX said on 14 November at 05:44 UTC that the Ship and its heatshield were healthy and that teams were still planning a return-to-launch-site catch at Starbase about 22.5 hours after launch. That catch is still a go/no-go, not a result.
The tower has never caught a Starship. It has caught a Super Heavy booster three times, on Flights 5, 7 and 8. This flight will not be a dual catch: the booster is already in the Gulf.

sections.title: Flight 15 so far
sections.lead: Checked 14 Nov 2026, 09:14 UTC. Ship 42 is still in orbit. The Saturday catch has not happened yet.

points.title: Lift-off
points.text: Flight 15 lifted off from Pad 2 at about 4:47 p.m. CT (22:47 UTC) on 13 Nov 2026, two minutes after the published window opened, according to Space.com's live coverage of SpaceX's webcast.

points.title: Hot-staging
points.text: SpaceX: hot-staging separation. Starship's Raptor engines ignited, and Super Heavy began boosting back toward Starbase for a catch.

points.title: Booster diverted
points.text: SpaceX: Super Heavy diverted to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf.

points.title: Orbit, second time
points.text: SpaceX: Starship performed its orbital insertion burn and entered orbit of Earth for the second time.

points.title: 26 Starlink V3s out
points.text: SpaceX: payload deploy complete. All 26 Starlink V3 satellites are in orbit.

points.title: Still go for a Ship catch
points.text: SpaceX at 05:44 UTC on 14 Nov, nearly seven hours after lift-off: Starship and its heatshield are healthy, and teams are still monitoring systems ahead of a planned return-to-launch-site catch at Starbase about 22.5 hours after launch.

body: On 20 April 2023, Starship's first integrated flight tumbled and was terminated. Several flights since have ended in explosions. SpaceX kept flying. Flight 2 proved hot staging at this scale. Flight 4 was the first time the ship survived a controlled re-entry. On Flight 5 the tower chopsticks caught Super Heavy on the first try, and later flights repeated the catch.

body.text: The V3 ship and booster debuted on Flight 12, on 22 May 2026, flying on Raptor 3 engines. Flight 14, on 28 September, reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Flight 15, with Ship 42, lifted off from Pad 2 on Friday 13 November at about 4:47 p.m. CT (22:47 UTC), according to Space.com's live coverage of SpaceX's webcast. Super Heavy diverted to the Gulf. Ship 42 reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. SpaceX said on 14 Nov that the heatshield is healthy and a return-to-launch-site catch at Starbase is still planned about 22.5 hours after launch, according to SpaceX on X.

sections.title: Minute by minute: the flown Friday, the Saturday catch still ahead
sections.lead: The Ship catch is not on launch day. Flight 15 lifted off at about 4:47 p.m. CT on Friday, so Ship 42 is due back at the tower on Saturday afternoon, about 22 and a half hours later, if the team stays go. Alex R's 12 November video walks the whole profile using SpaceX's published timeline. Times in the video assumed lift-off at window open (4:45 p.m. CST); actual events run about two minutes later.

points.title: Friday: lift-off to payload
points.text: The video's Friday clock, assuming lift-off at 4:45 p.m. CST, runs Max Q, hot-staging, the booster catch attempt at about 4:51 p.m., then payload deploy of 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Actual Friday events followed that shape: lift-off, hot-staging, a diverted booster splashdown instead of a catch, then all 26 Starlink V3s out. Event times and engine counts in the video follow SpaceX's timeline; speed and altitude readouts are simulated.

points.title: Saturday: the Ship catch
points.text: After about 14 orbits at roughly 275 km and three go/no-go checks, the video's Saturday clock has a 10-second deorbit burn at 2:20 p.m. CST and the arms closing at 3:17:34 p.m. Fail a check and the ship comes down early in the ocean near Hawaii or Chile.

points.title: Catch is still a go/no-go
points.text: SpaceX at T+7 hours: the Ship and heatshield were healthy ahead of a planned Starbase catch about 22.5 hours after launch. The catch flies only if systems stay healthy.

embed.name: Alex R
embed.text:
The Starship catch everyone's waiting for won't happen on launch day.

If Flight 15 gets off the pad when the window opens on Friday, the ship isn't due back at the tower until Saturday afternoon. That's 22 and a half hours later.

I animated the whole flight, countdown to catch, straight off SpaceX's own timeline. Every time below is local Starbase time (CST), assuming liftoff right at window open.

FRIDAY
4:45:00 PM · Liftoff on 33 Raptors. The window closes at 6:00
4:45:58 PM · Max Q
4:47:21 PM · Hot staging. The ship lights its engines while it's still attached to the booster
4:47:26 PM · Booster flips and burns back toward Texas
4:51:35 PM · Booster catch attempt. If a health check fails, it goes into the Gulf instead
4:53:09 PM · Ship engines off. Right now it's on a path that would drop it safely into the ocean
5:11:10 PM · One Raptor fires for 20 seconds to put it in orbit. That only happens if the ship is healthy
5:20:01 PM · The slot door opens and 26 Starlink V3 satellites slide out, one by one
6:02:40 PM · Last one's out

OVERNIGHT
Then it just waits. About 14 laps of the planet at roughly 275 km, with three go/no-go checks: 6:12 PM Friday, midnight, and 1:26 PM Saturday. Fail one and the ship comes down early in the ocean near Hawaii or Chile.

SATURDAY
2:20:57 PM · 10-second deorbit burn
2:55:46 PM · Hits the atmosphere belly first and the heat shield starts to glow
3:15:13 PM · Below the speed of sound, falling flat, steering with its 4 flaps
3:17:16 PM · 3 engines relight and it flips upright
3:17:26 PM · Down to 2 engines
3:17:33 PM · Down to 1
3:17:34 PM · The arms close

What I'll be watching:
• The booster relight. On Flight 14 only 11 of its 13 landing engines came back
• The ship's engines on the way up. Flight 14 lost a vacuum Raptor on ascent
• Entry. Controllers can still end the flight here by tumbling the ship
• 3 sea-level Raptors relighting after 22 hours in space. That's the big one

If both catches work, it's the first time an orbital rocket has ever been fully recovered. It still needs final FAA approval, and every time above moves if the launch slips.

Event times and engine counts in the video follow SpaceX's timeline. The speed and altitude readouts are simulated.

sections.title: Why this ship
sections.lead: The hardware work that is public is the static-fire campaign and catch tests on Pad 2.

points.text: SpaceX said on 28 Oct 2026 that Ship 42 "performed a full duration, six-engine static fire, and fired a single Raptor engine to simulate a deorbit burn." NASASpaceflight and Next Spaceflight put the single-engine burn on 26 Oct and the six-engine fire, about 60 seconds, on 27 Oct, both at Massey's.

On 11 and 12 September, Ship 42 was lifted by the Pad 2 chopsticks in catch-related tests, as seen in LabPadre and NASASpaceflight footage. Teams also connected the ship quick-disconnect arm several times.

On SpaceX's 20 Oct earnings call, Musk said the company will "attempt to catch both the booster and the ship" on Flight 15, and that "it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight." If both catches work, he said that would be "the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered."

sections.title: The tower for a Ship catch
sections.lead: Pad 2's tower is not the same machine that caught Super Heavy on earlier flights. SpaceX's May update covers shorter chopsticks, electromechanical actuators and a strengthened ship quick-disconnect. Alex R's 11 November post on X walks through the roof, the shorter arms and why they matter for Friday's Ship catch.

points.text: SpaceX's 12 May 2026 update on Pad 2 said the chopsticks are now shorter, "allowing faster motion to better track vehicles during catch operations." The main actuators changed from hydraulic to electromechanical "to improve speed, redundancy, and reliability." The ship quick-disconnect arm "has been strengthened, repackaged, and now rotates farther away from the rocket during launch."
points.title: What SpaceX has said

points.text: The Pad 2 tower now has a roof with protective cladding. Alex R's 11 November post reads that as a Ship-catch change: the vehicle comes in belly-first, flips upright and fires its Raptors beside the tower, and that burn can throw exhaust at the cables that move the chopsticks. That purpose is our analysis, not a SpaceX line. The same post says the roof went on late in construction and that SpaceX plans one for Pad 1; SpaceX has not published either.
points.title: A roof on the tower

points.text: The arms are two full truss sections shorter than the originals. The 11 November post's reading is that Boosters 12, 14 and 15 were all caught on the inner part of the arms, close to the tower, so the unused outer end came off. The old ship lifting pins are gone; Block 3 ships are not lifted that way.
points.title: Shorter arms

points.text: After a catch the ship still has leftover cryogenic propellant. The 11 November post's reading is that the stronger Pad 2 quick-disconnect arm swings in so that propellant can be drained before anyone inspects the vehicle or flies it again. SpaceX connected that arm to Ship 42 in September, as seen in the catch-related tests above; calling that a drain rehearsal is our reading.
points.title: Draining the Ship after a catch

embed.name: Alex R
embed.text:
SpaceX put a roof on its Starship launch tower, and it's there because of Friday's ship catch.

When Starship comes home, it falls belly-first, then flips upright and fires its Raptors to slow down right next to the tower. That burn can throw exhaust at the top of the tower, which is where the cables that move the chopstick arms run. So the Pad 2 tower got a roof covered in protective cladding. It went on late in construction, and SpaceX plans to add one to the Pad 1 tower too.

The arms changed as well. They're two full truss sections shorter than the originals, because Boosters 12, 14 and 15 were all caught on the inner part of the arms, close to the tower. The outer end never got used. The old ship lifting pins are gone too, since Block 3 ships don't get lifted that way anymore, and Pad 2 uses electromechanical actuators.

Then there's the quick disconnect arm, which is stronger on Pad 2. After a catch, the ship still has leftover super-cold propellant on board. This arm swings in and plugs into the ship so it can be drained before anyone inspects it or flies it again. SpaceX already rehearsed this with Ship 42, the Flight 15 ship, back in September.

Flight 15 is targeting Friday, Nov 13, if the FAA signs off. If it goes to plan, this tower catches its first Starship.

sections.title: What to watch on Ship 42
sections.lead: Times below are SpaceX's published Flight 15 profile, not a flown clock. The booster catch did not happen; Super Heavy diverted to the Gulf. Ship 42's own catch, if the team stays go, is more than 22 hours after lift-off.

timeline.title: Starship engine cutoff
timeline.text: Hot-staging is at about T+2:21; the Ship then burns until engine cutoff eight minutes after lift-off.

timeline.title: Payload deploy
timeline.text: SpaceX deployed all 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Three of them carry cameras to scan the heat shield and send the pictures down.

timeline.title: Deorbit burn
timeline.text: SpaceX lists return checks over Hawaii and Chile during the coast (early Hawaii, mid Chile, final Hawaii).

timeline.title: Entry, then landing burn and catch at about T+22:32:34
timeline.text: SpaceX says the Ship will only fly that profile if systems critical for re-entry, the landing burn and the tower approach are healthy.

sections.title: Why the heat shield matters
sections.lead: Bringing Ship 42 home intact means surviving re-entry. SpaceX's Flight 15 page is specific about what this heat shield is testing.

points.text: SpaceX says the heat shield takes the Flight 14 changes: extra retention on tiles most at risk of coming off during ascent, and work on paths that let plasma get behind the tiles. A large portion uses a curved tile meant to cut heating in the gaps.

Thousands of small hexagonal tiles cover the Ship's windward side. Because the Ship is mostly a plain cylinder, most tiles can share one shape and the rest are machined to fit, CNBC reported in August 2021.
Most tiles are attached mechanically rather than glued, and SpaceX makes them in-house, according to Air & Space (December 2021).

SpaceX posted the landing burn and splashdown of Super Heavy Booster 22.
SpaceX: Starship is in a long coast around Earth. Teams will monitor systems for the next ~21 hours. Early deorbit options remain, but all systems were looking good at that time.
SpaceX: payload deploy complete. All 26 Starlink V3 satellites are in orbit.
Elon Musk: live Starship video from space.
SpaceX: Starship performed its orbital insertion burn and entered orbit of Earth for the second time.
SpaceX: Super Heavy has diverted to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf.
SpaceX: liftoff of Starship. Space.com's live coverage of the webcast put T-0 at about 4:47 p.m. CT (22:47 UTC).

Alex R posted a minute-by-minute Flight 15 animation on X, using SpaceX's published timeline. If the window opens on time, the Ship catch is Saturday afternoon, about 22 and a half hours after Friday lift-off. Times are local Starbase (CST) and move if the launch slips.

Re-checked SpaceX's Flight 15 mission page on 13 Nov 2026: still as soon as Friday 13 November from Pad 2, 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC), 75-minute window, pending regulatory approval. Dual catch, 26 Starlink V3, more than 22 hours, webcast about 30 minutes before liftoff. This is a re-check, not a new date.

SpaceX: Ship 42 moved to the Starbase pad ahead of launch. The Flight 15 window is still as soon as Friday 13 November, 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC), 75 minutes, pending regulatory approval. Webcast about 30 minutes before liftoff. No FAA licence is published.

Alex R's 11 November post on X walks through Pad 2's new roof, shorter chopsticks and stronger quick-disconnect arm. The roof purpose, Pad 1 plan, truss cut and drain-after-catch reading are ours, not a SpaceX line. SpaceX's May Pad 2 update is linked in the tower section.
Re-checked SpaceX's Flight 15 mission page: the window is still as soon as Friday 13 November, 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC), 75 minutes, pending regulatory approval. No FAA licence is published.
SpaceX published the Flight 15 mission page: as soon as Friday 13 November from Pad 2, pending regulatory approval. Dual catch, 26 Starlink V3, more than 22 hours, first Ship return-to-launch-site.

SpaceX's 7 Nov update, "Returning Starship to the Launch Site", says Flight 15 will attempt the first Ship catch at Starbase. Controllers will only commit to that catch if internally developed, FAA-approved return conditions are met.
SpaceX said Ship 42's static fires are complete: a full-duration six-engine fire and a single-engine deorbit-burn simulation.
Elon Musk quoted SpaceX's post: "As the prophecy foretold, Starship 42 will be the first tower catch."
NASASpaceflight and Next Spaceflight logged Ship 42's six-engine static fire at Massey's on 27 Oct, about 5:46 p.m. ET (2:46 p.m. PT), roughly 60 seconds.
NASASpaceflight's live coverage and Next Spaceflight's test log put Ship 42's single-engine deorbit-burn simulation at Massey's on 26 Oct at about 10:17 p.m. ET (7:17 p.m. PT).
SpaceX confirmed a full-duration 33-engine static fire of Booster 22, the Flight 15 Super Heavy, on Pad 2.
